topics.title: Design Library Management System
Uber
topics.concepts: Geo-indexing, location updates, matching, distributed systems
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Design Uber's backend for matching riders with nearby drivers in real time: ingest millions of driver location updates, find the best nearby available driver within seconds, handle offers and acceptance, track trips, and price dynamically. The focus is **geo-indexing**, **high-frequency location updates**, **matching** and **distributed consistency** (one driver, one trip).

## Requirements

**Functional**
- Drivers publish location every ~4 s while online. Riders request a ride and get an ETA and a price.
- Match within a few seconds. The driver accepts or declines. Live tracking for both parties.
- Trip lifecycle, fare calculation, payments.

**Non-functional**
- Matching p99 < a few seconds. Location writes are high-volume but each one is cheap and short-lived.
- A driver must never be double-assigned.

**Scale:** 5M online drivers ÷ 4 s ≈ **1.25M location writes/s**. Ride requests are only ~10k/s, but each queries nearby drivers.

## 1. Scope and selected ownership

I support live driver availability, ride requests, matching and trip lifecycle. I choose a geo index for candidates and a transactional assignment authority for driver exclusivity. ETA ranking can use a routing service; straight-line distance only narrows candidates.

## 2. APIs and state

```text
PUT /drivers/{id}/location {sessionId,seq,point,accuracy,observedAt}
POST /trips {pickup,destination,requestId}
POST /offers/{id}/accept -> assigned | expired | conflict
Assignment: driverId UNIQUE(active), tripId UNIQUE(active), lease/version
Location: driverId,sessionId,seq,point,lastSeen
```

Ingestion validates identity and monotonic session sequence, conditionally updates latest location and cell membership, then expires stale observations. Dispatch scores fresh eligible candidates and sends bounded offers. Acceptance claims the driver/trip pair atomically, and returns the existing result on a true retry. Driver migration between cells may temporarily duplicate search entries but never assignment authority. One million drivers at four-second cadence generates 250,000 updates/s; that drives partitioning and adaptive cadence. Trip events persist separately from location observations; offer timeout and dispatcher crash are recovered using original identities and pending state.

## 3. Final design diagram

[![Uber: Rider and driver apps location updates Location ingestion; Location ingestion latest positions Geo candidate index; Dispatch service nearby search Geo candidate index; Dispatch service offers Offer stream; Offer stream push Rider and driver apps; Dispatch service claim Assignment authority; Assignment authority trip ownership Trip store](designs/hld-9.svg)](designs/hld-9.svg)

A **location index** supports nearby candidates. A **trip owner** serializes trip changes. A **driver availability record** prevents conflicting assignments. Geographic partitioning reduces search scope, but riders and drivers cross cell and region boundaries.

## 4. Critical operation: worked execution

![The fast location index proposes drivers; assignment establishes ownership.](lessons/hld-9-flow.svg)

*The fast location index proposes drivers; assignment establishes ownership.*

![Movement must not create duplicate assignment authority.](lessons/hld-9-failure.svg)

*Movement must not create duplicate assignment authority.*

### Calculate freshness and load

One million active drivers sending every four seconds produces 250,000 location updates/s. Sending every second quadruples ingest load without guaranteeing four times better pickup decisions. Choose cadence using motion, battery, network and freshness requirements. Index recent observations with expiry rather than retaining every GPS point forever in the hot search store.

## 5. Detailed decisions, algorithms and failure behaviour

### Architecture

- **Location service:** stateless ingest (WebSocket or UDP-ish) that updates an **in-memory geo index** sharded by region or cell. Latest position only; history goes asynchronously to Kafka for analytics and ETA models.
- **Geo index:** a hexagonal grid (Uber's **H3**) or geohash. `cell → set of available drivers`. Nearby search queries the rider's cell plus k-ring neighbours and widens if needed.
- **Matching (dispatch) service:** gets candidates, computes the real ETA (road network, not straight-line distance), picks the best, and **atomically reserves** the driver (CAS on driver state in Redis or the owning shard) before sending the offer.
- **Trip service:** a durable state machine in a transactional DB, publishing events for tracking, notifications and billing.

### Key design decisions & trade-offs

**1. Geohash vs. quadtree vs. H3.** Geohash is simple string prefixes but has edge distortions and cells of unequal neighbour distance. A quadtree adapts to density but is harder to shard. **H3 hexagons** have uniform neighbour distances, which makes them good for k-ring search and surge zones.

**2. Don't put 1.25M writes/s in a database.** Location is ephemeral: keep the latest position in memory (Redis GEO or custom sharded in-memory services) and replicate for failover. Losing a few seconds of positions is fine, because drivers will send the next update.

**3. Sharding by geography.** City or region shards keep matching local and cache-friendly. Hot spots (an airport at a concert's end) need finer cells or dynamic splitting.

**4. Reserving the driver.** Matching might pick the same driver for two riders concurrently. A CAS from `AVAILABLE` to `DISPATCHING` on the owning shard ensures one winner. Offer timeouts release the driver.

**5. Batched matching.** Instead of greedily matching each request immediately, collect requests over a ~1–2 s window and solve a bipartite assignment that minimises total ETA. That gives better global outcomes and is what large platforms do.

**6. Surge pricing.** Compute the supply/demand ratio per cell every minute from streaming counts, smooth it, and lock the quoted price for the rider for a few minutes.

### Scope, guarantees and sizing assumptions

**Correctness requirement:** A driver can own only one active ride; location search may be stale but assignment must be authoritative.

Assume 1 million online drivers publishing every 5 seconds: 200,000 location updates/s. At 200 bytes/update, about 40 MB/s raw ingress. Nearby search returns a bounded candidate set, not every driver in a city.

### API contracts and data ownership

```text
POST /ride-requests; POST /offers/{id}/accept; stream /drivers/{id}/location with sequence and timestamp
```

```text
Logical records (outline, not complete DDL):
driver_location(driver_id,cell,lat,lon,sequence,observed_at); availability(driver_id,active_trip,version); trip(id,status,offer_epoch)

Primary access/partitioning boundary:
geospatial cell for candidate discovery; driver_id/trip_id for authoritative assignment
```

### Build the architecture in stages

**Stage 3 — Partition and isolate.** Partition around geospatial cell for candidate discovery; driver_id/trip_id for authoritative assignment. Track ownership with a routing epoch or a database-native partition mechanism. Move virtual buckets or copy/backfill data with a verified cutover, rather than changing a modulo divisor and assuming records move themselves. Isolate bulk/background workloads from the latency-sensitive path and test the busiest tenant independently.

### Trace the critical request

Ingest sequenced GPS samples; discard outdated samples; maintain cell indexes; query neighboring cells; rank viable candidates by estimated pickup cost; issue bounded offers; atomically claim driver and trip; then publish the assignment and start tracking.

### Deep dive: the decision that changes this system

Geohash/H3-like cells reduce search candidates but cell boundaries require neighbor expansion. Straight-line distance is a cheap first filter, not an ETA. Time-stamped location and TTL detect stale availability estimates; they do not replace the assignment transaction.

### Failure and race-condition walkthrough

Two matchers receive acceptance from the same driver for different trips. An authoritative compare-and-set rejects one, while an epoch rejects delayed offers. Retry dispatch without duplicating confirmed rides.

### Security, tenancy and lifecycle

### Trade-offs and a starting recommendation

City/regional ownership limits latency and data movement; cross-border trips need handoff semantics. Matching quality improves with batch optimization but waiting too long harms rider latency.

Time-to-match, assignment conflicts, stale-location fraction, pickup ETA error, location ingest lag and driver/rider cancellation rate.

**Test matrix:** Hot city center, cell-boundary query, stale GPS, reordered updates, simultaneous acceptance, cancellation race and regional ownership handoff.

### Follow-up questions with answers

**What cannot be eventually consistent here?** The operation establishing this guarantee: A driver can own only one active ride; location search may be stale but assignment must be authoritative.

**What is the first scaling pressure to test?** Use the actual workload: Assume 1 million online drivers publishing every 5 seconds: 200,000 location updates/s. At 200 bytes/update, about 40 MB/s raw ingress. Nearby search returns a bounded candidate set, not every driver in a city.

**Which failure would invalidate the naive design?** Two matchers receive acceptance from the same driver for different trips. An authoritative compare-and-set rejects one, while an epoch rejects delayed offers. Retry dispatch without duplicating confirmed rides.

**Why not introduce every distributed component immediately?** City/regional ownership limits latency and data movement; cross-border trips need handoff semantics. Matching quality improves with batch optimization but waiting too long harms rider latency.

**How would you demonstrate the design works?** Hot city center, cell-boundary query, stale GPS, reordered updates, simultaneous acceptance, cancellation race and regional ownership handoff. Keep the expected invariant and recovery outcome visible in the results.

### Further reading

- [PostgreSQL isolation and anomalies](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html).
- [Apache Kafka delivery and transaction design](https://kafka.apache.org/41/design/design/).
- [Redis rate-limiter design](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/use-cases/rate-limiter/) for atomic shared-state examples.

### Work through stale data

A location event with sequence 108 must not be overwritten by delayed event 107. Compare sequence/time under the device-session policy; timestamps alone can be unreliable if the phone clock changes. A nearby driver with a stale last-seen time can be excluded or penalized before offering.

Assignment uses leases or transactions with explicit identities. If a dispatcher stops after claiming the driver but before replying, reconciliation must resolve the original assignment rather than making the driver permanently busy. Keep fare quotes, live trip tracking and financial settlement as distinct workflows.

## 6. Interviewer follow-ups

**Does a geohash give road ETA?** No. It narrows candidates; road routing and traffic estimate actual travel time.

**Can a cache decide final driver exclusivity?** Only if it is explicitly the authoritative assignment system with appropriate durability/atomicity—not merely a search cache.

## 7. Closing answer

Geographic indexing makes matching efficient but the assignment authority makes it correct. I reject stale position updates, keep offers expiring/versioned and serialize driver/trip claims. Geographic cell boundaries therefore do not become duplicate assignment boundaries.

topics.title: Conversation Memory
topics.concepts: Chat memory, conversation IDs, persistent memory, context management
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Explain conversation memory for LLM apps: LLMs are stateless, so "memory" means deciding what past conversation (and long-term user facts) to send with each request. Cover Spring AI's `ChatMemory`, conversation IDs, persistence, window and summarisation strategies, and managing the context budget.

## Requirements

- Why the model "forgets", and where memory actually lives (your app).
- Short-term (conversation) vs. long-term (user facts, preferences) memory.
- Spring AI: `ChatMemory`, `MessageWindowChatMemory`, chat memory repositories (in-memory, JDBC, Cassandra, Neo4j), memory advisors.
- Conversation IDs, multi-user isolation, persistence, retention.
- Context-window management: windowing, summarisation, retrieval-based memory.

## 1. Selected memory model

I choose tenant/user/conversation-scoped message storage and serialized turns per conversation. Recent complete turns are selected by token budget, with optional versioned summaries for older discussion. The authoritative conversation record stays separate from the prompt window.

## 2. Turn contract and consistency

```text
POST /conversations/{id}/turns {requestId,expectedVersion,question}
 -> completedAnswer | conflict | denied | partialFailure
Conversation: tenantId,userId,id,version,retentionPolicy
Message: conversationId,sequence,role,content,state,requestId
```

I resolve the submitted ID against authenticated ownership, acquire the conversation turn lease/version, select bounded history and call the model. Final output and the committed turn are recorded once. Two tabs using version 7 cannot silently append unrelated answers based on the same old history; one conflicts or waits under the chosen serialization policy. A failed stream remains partial, not a successful assistant memory turn.

Ten 600-token turns consume roughly 6,000 tokens before instructions/evidence/output. I preserve coherent tool-call/result groups when pruning. Summaries can omit or distort constraints, so allergies, permissions and financial facts belong in typed authoritative state. Deletion invalidates messages, summaries, vectors and relevant caches, rather than only hiding the visible transcript.

## 3. Final design diagram

[![Conversation Memory: Authenticated principal owned scope Conversation service; Conversation service ordered history Message store; Message store selects messages Memory selector; Memory selector token bound Context budgeter; Context budgeter request context ChatClient; ChatClient completed turn Turn journal](designs/ai-9.svg)](designs/ai-9.svg)

A **conversation ID** identifies stored history, a **memory window** selects retained messages, and a **summary** compresses older content with possible information loss. A user's ownership of the conversation must be verified independently of the ID they submit.

## 4. Critical operation: worked execution

![Only selected, owned history enters the model request.](lessons/ai-9-flow.svg)

*Only selected, owned history enters the model request.*

![Conversation scoping is a security decision before the model call.](lessons/ai-9-failure.svg)

*Conversation scoping is a security decision before the model call.*

### Work a context window

Ten turns averaging 600 tokens are about 6,000 tokens before system messages, evidence and output reserve. Keeping the last ten **messages** is not the same as the last ten **turns**, and neither directly limits tokens. Budget actual selected context and preserve complete tool-call/result pairs where required.

```text
Storage scope: tenantId + userId + conversationId
Request context: instructions + selected history + question + evidence
Persisted turn: requestId + sequence + final output + state
```

## 5. Detailed decisions, algorithms and failure behaviour

### Mechanism and rationale

**Design question:** How can a chat remember prior turns without leaking another user’s conversation or exhausting context?

Persisted conversation history is application state. Each model request includes a selected view of it; provider-side caches do not replace this store. Window memory drops old turns; summaries compress them; retrieval can recover relevant past facts but adds ranking and privacy concerns.

### Architecture and contracts

```text
Authenticate conversation ownership -> append user turn -> select bounded history -> model/tool turns -> validate -> append final assistant turn

Application contracts (design outline):
ConversationKey(tenant,user,conversation); Message(role,body,sequence,toolCallId); MemoryPolicy(maxTokens,retention)
```

A chat-memory advisor can select and insert messages, but the application must authorize the conversation before invoking it. Use the API matching the pinned Spring AI baseline; newer session APIs have different names.

### Worked reasoning and capacity example

Twenty turns averaging 500 tokens each already consume 10,000 tokens before task instructions, retrieval and output allowance. Summaries should have their own budget and revision, not grow without bound.

### Java and Spring AI implementation outline

```java
record ConversationKey(String tenant, String user, String conversation) {}
interface ConversationRepository {
  java.util.List<String> authorizedHistory(ConversationKey key, int maxTokens);
}
// Persist roles/tool-call relationships in the real message schema.
```

### Design decisions and alternatives

Key memory by tenant plus authenticated user plus conversation, not a user-supplied conversation ID alone. Store raw history separately from derived summaries, with deletion and retention rules for each.

### Failure scenario and safe recovery

Two tabs append to one conversation concurrently. Sequence or version the append, and build the response against a known history snapshot. A tool result must match the tool call that produced it; dropping one half creates invalid context.

### Security, privacy and provenance

A summary generated by an LLM can turn uncertainty into a false permanent fact. Keep provenance and allow users to correct retained information.


**Verification criteria:** Measure cross-user leakage, retained facts, summary drift, context tokens and correctness after truncation. Use adversarial conversations that try to claim another tenant’s identity.

### Further reading

- [Spring AI 1.1 ChatClient and request APIs](https://docs.spring.io/spring-ai/reference/1.1/api/chatclient.html).
- [Spring AI tool-execution boundary](https://docs.spring.io/spring-ai/reference/1.1/api/tools.html).
- [MCP specification, versioned protocol concepts](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18).
- [Original RAG research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401) and [Transformer research](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) for background rather than framework instructions.

### Work through concurrent turns

Two tabs send follow-ups to the same conversation simultaneously. Without sequencing, both can answer against the same old history and append in an arbitrary order. Serialize per conversation, use optimistic version checks or explicitly represent branching. Do not pretend arrival timestamps alone define user intent.

A summary can accidentally omit an allergy, a constraint or a quoted negation. Keep critical application facts in typed authoritative state; do not entrust them only to a generated summary. Deletion must consider messages, summaries, vectors and caches under the retention policy.

## 6. Interviewer follow-ups

**Can a conversation ID supplied by the model establish ownership?** No. Resolve it against authenticated application identity.

**Does pruning history change old stored messages?** It need not; prompt selection and storage retention are separate policies.

## 7. Closing answer

Conversation memory is application-selected context, not model retraining. I enforce ownership before reading history, order concurrent turns explicitly and keep critical business facts out of lossy summaries. Retention/deletion covers every representation used by the application.
